query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, exposure to intermediate service temperatures activates rapid, thermally driven nanosegregation of principal elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, and Mn in fcc HEAs) along grain boundaries. This nanocluster formation reduces local grain‐boundary cohesion, triggering a transition from ductile transgranular to brittle intergranular failure—an embrittlement mechanism distinct from conventional alloys where impurity segregation or large intermetallic precipitates dominate.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi or a similar compositionally complex HEA) with uniformly distributed elements and no preexisting secondary phase precipitates.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled aging/deformation at intermediate temperatures (e.g., ~650–700°C) under high strain rate loading to induce potential grain-boundary nanosegregation.
generation.conditions: Testing in an inert environment (to rule out oxidation effects) at intermediate service temperatures (around 650–700°C) and at strain rates typical of demanding engineering applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions where nanoclusters of principal elements form via rapid segregation under thermal activation.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation at intermediate temperatures drives the diffusion and nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries. This localized compositional inhomogeneity diminishes cohesive strength at GBs, favoring intergranular crack initiation over the ductile, transgranular deformation normally observed in the initial state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (room-temperature ductile behavior with transgranular fracture), the unmodified HEA will exhibit a marked reduction in toughness at intermediate temperatures, with SEM/TEM analyses revealing intergranular brittle fracture linked to observable nanosegregation at grain boundaries. In a controlled comparison with samples engineered to host preexisting secondary (e.g., Cr-rich) precipitates that capture embrittling elements, the latter should show improved ductility at the same temperatures.
generation.baseline: The alloy in its as-cast or homogenized condition exhibits high tensile ductility and predominantly ductile, transgranular fracture at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under intermediate temperatures (∼650–700°C) and high strain rates. At much higher temperatures where nanoclusters might dissolve or at cryogenic temperatures where diffusion is suppressed, alternative mechanisms are likely to govern the fracture behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics and composition of the nanosegregation, as well as its quantitative impact on GB cohesion, remain to be fully characterized. Detection of nanoclusters may be challenging, and variations in local alloy chemistry could affect the threshold for embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens with identical, single-phase microstructures. For Set A, retain the homogeneous state. For Set B, introduce controlled preexisting Cr-rich precipitates at grain boundaries (via an annealing protocol designed to nucleate such secondary phases). Subject both sets to tensile testing at an intermediate temperature (~700°C) and at high strain rates in an inert atmosphere. Conduct fractographic analysis (using SEM and TEM) and perform elemental mapping (via atom probe tomography or EDS line scans) along grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture surface morphology (to distinguish intergranular vs transgranular failure)
Grain-boundary composition profiles (to detect nanosegregation vs precipitate absorption of embrittling elements)
Mechanical properties such as tensile ductility and toughness.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the unmodified and the precipitate-engineered samples display similar fracture modes (i.e., predominantly intergranular brittle fracture) and grain-boundary analyses show no significant difference in nanosegregation of principal elements, then the hypothesis that rapid nanosegregation-induced GB decohesion causes brittleness is not supported. Similarly, if ductility loss does not correlate with the presence of nanoclusters at GBs, the mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are emerging materials with potential for use under extreme conditions. As a newly developed material system, a comprehensive understanding of their long-term stability under potential service temperatures remains to be established. This study examined a titanium-vanadium-niobium-tantalum alloy, a promising RHEA known for its superior high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility. Using a combination of advanced analytical microscopies, Calculation of Phase Diagrams (CALPHAD) software, and nanoindentation, we investigated the evolution of its microstructure and mechanical properties upon aging at 700°C. Trace interstitials such as oxygen and nitrogen, initially contributing to solid solution strengthening, promote phase segregation during thermal aging. As a result of the depletion of solute interstitials within the metal matrix, a progressive softening is observed in the alloy as a function of aging time. This study, therefore, underscores the need for a better control of impurities in future development and application of RHEAs. cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement.
